term_table.greek_sentence: ὑπὲρ ἧς ἀναισχυντεῖ ὁ χορὸς αὐτοῦ, περί τε χολῆς καὶ οὔρου διακρίσεως, ἀναδόσεώς τε καὶ ἄλλων τοιούτων ἀλλόκοτα λέγειν ὑπέμεινεν, ἔτι τε τοῖς φαινομένοις ἐναντία τίθεται, καθάπερ ἐδείξαμεν ἔμπροσθεν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: It is concerning this power that his chorus behaves shamelessly, and has brought itself to say outlandish things about the separation of bile and of urine, about distribution (anadosis) and other such matters, and moreover it posits things contrary to the phenomena, as we showed before.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Concerning this power his chorus behaves shamelessly, and has brought itself to say outlandish things about the separation of bile and of urine, about distribution and other such matters; and moreover he posits things contrary to the phenomena, as we showed earlier.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: μέλας ( μέλας Rhian. 58 , where μέγας is corrupt for μέλας), μέλαινα, μέλαν; gen. μέλανος, μελαίνης, μέλανος, etc.; Ep. dat. μείλανι (metri gr.) Il. 24.79 : Aeol. nom. μέλαις, from Μέλανς, Choerob. in Theod. 1.123 , Greg.Cor. p.599 S. , hence restored in Sapph. 57 :—black, dark: in Hom. generally, dark in colour, οἶνος Od. 5.265 ; μέλαν αἷμα, κῦμα, Il. 4.149 , 23.693 ; γαῖα μέλαινα 2.699 , cf. Sapph. Supp. 5.2 ; ὕδωρ μέλαν Αἰσήποιο Il. 2.825 , cf. Od. 4.359 , νηῦς μ., from its being pitched over, Il. 1.300 , al.; of men, dark, swarthy, μέλανας δὲ ἀνδρικοὺς ἰδεῖν Pl. R. 474e ; ἰσχυρός τις ἦν, μ. D. 21.71 ; τὰ μ. black marks about the ears of dogs, X. Cyn. 5.23 . dark, murky, ἕσπερος Od. 1.423 ; εὐφρόνα Pi. N. 7.3 . metaph., black, dark, θάνατος Il. 2.834 , etc.; κήρ ib. 859 , etc.; ὀδύναι 4.117 , etc. (the origin of the metaphor is seen in the phrases θανάτου μ. νέφος, ἄχεος νεφέλη μ., 16 . 350 , 18.22 ); μ. τύχα, ἀρά, A. Supp. 89 (lyr.), Th. 832 (lyr.); Ἐρινύς ib. 993 (lyr.), cf. Eu. 52 ; ἄτα Id. Ag. 769 (lyr.); Ἄρης ib. 1511 (lyr.); Ἅιδης S. OT 29 ; Ἅιδου μ. ἀνάγκα E. Hipp. 1388 (lyr.), etc.; ἡμέραι μέλαιναι, = Lat. dies atri, Plu. Luc. 27 . of the voice, indistinct, Arist. Top. 106a25 , Philostr. VA 4.44 ; βραχὺ καὶ μ. φώνημα, of Nero, D.C. 61.20 . dark, obscure, enigmatical, ἱστορίη AP 11.347 ( Phil. ). of character, dark, malignant, μ. φρήν, καρδία, Sol. 42.4 , Pi. Fr. 123.4 ; μ. ἄνθρωποι Plu. 2.12d ; μ. ἦθος M. Ant. 4.28 . Comp. μελάντερος, α, ον , blacker, very black, τοῦ δ' οὔ τι μελάντερον ἔπλετο ἔσθος Il. 24.94 : prov. of thick darkness, [νέφοσ] μελάντερον ἠΰτε πίσσα (v. ἠΰτε) 4.277 : Sup. μελάντατος Hp. VC 14 , Ar. Fr. 580 , etc.:— Comp. also μελανώτερος Str. 16.4.12 : Sup. μελαινότατος AP 11.68 ( Lucill. ), Epigr.Gr. 320.4 (Thyatira). μέλαινα (sc. νοῦσος), ἡ, Medic., of diseases causing black secretions (such as melaena), Hp. Morb. 2.73 . μέλαν, τό , v. sub voc. (Cf. Skt. málam 'dirt', malinás 'dirty', Lett. melns 'black'.)
term_table.lsj_first_sense_gloss: where μέγας is corrupt for μέλας)
term_table.greek_sentence: εἰ γὰρ ἀληθὴς ἡ ὑπόθεσις αὕτη, πλείστη μὲν ἡ σύμπασα κένωσις ἐπὶ τοῖς τῆς μελαίνης ἀγωγοῖς, ἐλαχίστη δὲ ἐπὶ τοῖς τῶν ὀῤῥωδῶν [339] περιττωμάτων ἔσται.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For if this hypothesis is true, the total evacuation will be greatest with the drugs that draw black bile, and least with those that draw the serous [339] residues.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For if this hypothesis is true, the total evacuation will be greatest with the drugs that draw off black [bile], and least with those that draw off the serous [339] residues.

term_table.english_sentence_B: For if this hypothesis is true, the total evacuation will be greatest with the drugs that draw off black [bile], and least with those that draw off the serous [339] residues.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ὑδραγωγ-έω, conduct or convey water, Ostr.Bodl. iii 390 (ii A. D., dub.):— Pass. , ὕδωρ ὑδραγωγεῖται v.l. in Str. 13.1.67 , cf. PRyl. 157.19 (ii A. D.).
term_table.greek_sentence: καὶ μὴν δείξω σοι μυριάκις, ἐὰν θελήσῃς, ὦ σοφιστὰ, κᾂν νῦν γοῦν θεάσασθαι τὰ τῆς τέχνης ἔργα, τοῖς μὲν ὑδραγωγοῖς φαρμάκοις ἑπομένην ἀεὶ πλείστην κένωσιν, τοῖς δὲ τὴν μέλαιναν ἐκκαθαίρουσιν ἐλαχίστην.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And yet I shall show you ten thousand times, sophist, if you are willing, now at any rate if never before, to look at the works of the art, that a very great evacuation always follows the hydragogue drugs, and a very small one follows those that purge out black bile.
term_table.english_sentence_B: And yet I will show you ten thousand times over, sophist, if you are willing, now at least, to behold the works of the art, that the greatest evacuation always follows the hydragogue drugs and the least follows those that purge out black [bile].

term_table.lsj_entry_text: φάρμακον [v. sub fin.], τό, drug, whether healing or noxious: in Hom. the sense is freq. determined by an epith., φάρμακα, πολλὰ μὲν ἐσθλὰ . . , πολλὰ δὲ λυγρά Od. 4.230 ; τόδε φ. ἐσθλόν 10.287 , cf. 292 ; φ. ἤπια, ὀδυνήφατα (v. infr. 2 ); κακὰ φ. ib. 213 ; φ. λυγρά ib. 236 ; φ. οὐλόμενον ib. 394 ; ἀνδροφόνον 1.261 ; θυμοφθόρα φ. 2.329 ; so, after Hom. , προσανέα φ. Pi. P. 3.52 ; παιώνια A. Ag. 848 ; χρήσιμον Pl. R. 382c ; θανάσιμα Ph. Bel. 103.31 ; ὀλέθριον Luc. Herm. 62 . healing remedy, medicine, in Hom. mostly of those applied outwardly, ἐπιθήσει φάρμαχ' ἅ κεν παύσῃσι μελαινάων ὀδυνάων Il. 4.191 ; ἐπ' ἄρ' ἤπια φάρμακα πάσσε ib. 218 ; ὀδυνήφατα φ. πάσσων 5.401 , 900 , cf. 11.515 , 830 , 15.394 ; προσάλειφεν ἑκάστῳ φ. Od. 10.392 ; φ. περιαλείφειν Ar. Eq. 906 ; also of potions, πιὼν φάρμακ' Od. 10.326 ; φ. πεπωκώς Hdt. 4.160 , cf. Pi. l. c.; παρὰ τοῦ ἰατροῦ Pl. R. 406d , cf. Grg. 467c ; φ. χριστόν E. Hipp. 516 ; ἔγχριστον Theoc. 11.1 ; ἐπίχριστον Str. 17.1.10 ; ἐπίπαστον Theoc. l. c.; καταπλαστόν Ar. Pl. 716 ; ποτόν E. Hipp. l.c.; freq. in Medic. writers, Sor. 1.4 , Gal. 6.265 , etc.; of medicines for cattle, PFlor. 222.11 (iii A. D.). c. gen. (v. infr. 11 ), φ. νόσου a medicine for it, remedy against it, A. Pr. 251 , 606 (lyr.); βηχός Phryn.Com. 60 : κεφαλῆς for a head-ache, Pl. Chrm. 155b ; στραγγουρίας Arist. HA 612b16 , cf. 624a16 ; μέθης Amphis 37 ; δίψης AP 6.170 ( Thyill. ); but ὑγιείας φ. a medicine to restore or maintain health, Aristid. Or. 37(2).11 . enchanted potion, philtre: hence, charm, spell, Od. 4.220 sq., Ar. Pl. 302 , Theoc. 2.15 , PSI 1.64.20 (i B. C.); φαρμάκοις τὸν ἄνδρ' ἔμηνεν Ar. Th. 561 ; τοιαῦτα ἔχω φ. such charms have I, Hdt. 3.85 , cf. Apoc. 9.21 . poison, S. Tr. 685 , E. Med. 385 ; πιεῖν τὸ φ. Antipho 6.15 , Pl. Phd. 57a , 115a ; φάρμακα ἐσβεβληκέναι ἐς τὰ φρέατα Th. 2.48 ; φ. δηλητήρια SIG 37 A 1 (Teos, v B. C.); τοξικὸν φ. BGU 21 ii 14 (iv A. D.). lye for laundering, Stud.Pal. 22.56.12 (iii A. D.). generally, remedy, cure, Hes. Op. 485 , Alc. 35 , etc.; μεῖζον . . τῆς νόσου τὸ φ. the cure too strong for, i. e. worse than, the disease, S. Fr. 589.4 , cf. Com.Adesp. 455 ; φ. πραΰ, of a bridle, Pi. O. 13.85 ; φ. τινι for a thing, Thgn. 1134 (pl.), Archil. 9 ; πρός τι Arist. Pol. 1321a16 ; ποττὸν ἔρωτα Theoc. 11.1 ; but most freq. φ. τινός remedy against . . χλαῖνα . . φ. ῥίγευς Hippon. 19 ; Ζεὺς πάντων φ. μοῦνος ἔχει Simon. 87 ; τὸ σιγᾶν φ. βλάβης ἔχω A. Ag. 548 ; φ. πόνων, λύπης, E. Ba. 283 , Fr. 1079 ; δόλοι . . χρείας ἀνάνδρου φ. ib. 288 ; φόβου Pl. Lg. 647e ; λήθης φάρμακα (of γράμματα) E. Fr. 578.1 ; v. εὐδιανός. c. gen. also, a means of producing something, φ. σωτηρίας Id. Ph. 893 ; μνήμης καὶ σοφίας φ. Pl. Phdr. 274e ; ὑπομνήσεως ib. 275a , cf. 230d ; ἀθανασίας Antiph. 86.6 ; ἡσυχίας Arist. Pol. 1273b23 ; φ. μανίας, of the oil applied to wrestlers, D.L. 1.104 . ἐπὶ θανάτῳ φ. ἑᾶς ἀρετᾶς εὑρέσθαι a remedy or consolation in his own virtue, Pi. P. 4.187 . dye, paint, colour, Emp. 23.3 , Hdt. 1.98 , A. Fr. 134 , Ar. Ec. 735 , Pl. R. 420c , Plt. 277c , PCair.Zen. 789.13 (iii B. C.), etc. chemical reagent, PLeid.X. 25 , PHolm. 13.46 , 22.10 , Ps.-Democr. ap. Zos.Alch. p.160 B. ; used by tanners, Sch. Ar. Eq. 44 , 368 .—Cf. φαρμάσσω. [μα; but μα in φαρμακός.]

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἀμαθ-ής, ές, (μαθεῖν) ignorant, stupid, Hdt. 1.33 , Democr. 169 , etc.; ἔθνεα ἀμαθέστατα Hdt. 4.46 ; ἀνὴρ πένης, εἰ καὶ γένοιτο μὴ ἀ. E. Supp. 421 , al., Ar. Nu. 135 ; ἀ. καὶ βδελυρός Id. Eq. 193 ; ἀμαθεστάτους πάντων ἀνθρώπων And. 2.2 ; ἀ. τὴν [ἐκείνων] ἀμαθίαν Pl. Ap. 22e ; opp. δεξιός, Th. 3.82 ; of animals, such as wild boars, unmanageable, θυμώδη καὶ ἀ. Arist. HA 488b14 : c. gen. rei, without knowledge of a thing, unlearned in it, -έστερος τοῦ καλοῦ E. Or. 417 ; λῃστείας Th. 4.41 , cf. 3.37 ; ἀ. περί τινος Pl. Erx. 394e ; τι La. 194d ; πρός τι Lg. 679d . Adv. -θῶς ignorantly, through ignorance, ἥμαρτον E. Ph. 874 : Comp. -έστερον, τῶν νόμων ὑπεροψίας παιδεύεσθαι to be educated with too little learning to despise the laws, Th. 1.84 ; -έστερόν πως εἰπὲ καὶ σαφέστερον less learnedly, Ar. Ra. 1445 . of moral defects, unfeeling, inhuman, ἀ. τις εἶ θεός E. HF 347 . of things, ἀ. παρρησία boorish freedom of speech, E. Or. 905 ; ἀ. ῥώμη brute force, Id. Fr. 732 ; ἀ. δύναμις Plu. Demetr. 42 ; ἀ. φρόνημα barbarous pride, E. Heracl. 459 . not heard of, unknown, ἀ. ἔρρει E. Ion 916 . Adv. ἀμαθῶς, χωρῆσαι, of events, to take an unforeseen course, Th. 1.140 .
term_table.greek_sentence: Ὁ μὲν οὖν ἕλκεσθαι λέγων ὁμοτίμως ἅπαντας τοὺς χυμοὺς εἰς τοσοῦτον ἀναίσθητός τε καὶ ἀμαθής ἐστιν, ὁ δ’ ἀλλοιοῦσθαι θεασάσθω πάλιν εἰς ὅσον οὐδὲν διοίσει κατ’ αὐτὸν ἢ φλεβοτομεῖν ἢ καθαίρειν χολαγωγῷ φαρμάκῳ τὸν ἰκτεριῶντα.
term_table.english_sentence_A: So the one who says that all the humours are drawn alike is to this degree insensible and ignorant; and let the one who says that they are altered consider in turn to what extent, on his account, it will make no difference whether one phlebotomizes the jaundiced patient or purges him with a cholagogue drug.
term_table.english_sentence_B: So the one who says that all the humours are drawn equally is insensible and ignorant to this degree. As for the one who says that they are altered, let him see in his turn to what degree, on his view, it will make no difference whether one phlebotomises the jaundiced patient or purges him with a cholagogue drug.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: αἰσχρός, ά, όν, also ός, όν APl. 4.151 : (αἶσχος):—in Hom. , causing shame, dishonouring, reproachful, νείκεσσεν . . αἰσχροῖς ἐπέεσσιν Il. 3.38 , etc. Adv. αἰσχρῶς, ἐνένισπεν 23.473 . opp. καλός: of outward appearance, ugly, ill-favoured, of Thersites, Il. 2.216 , cf. h.Ap. 197 , Hdt. 1.196 ( Comp. ), etc. ; deformed, Hp. Art. 14 ( Sup. ); αἰσχρῶς χωλός with an ugly lameness, ib. 63 : but commonly, in moral sense, shameful, base, Hdt. 3.155 , A. Th. 685 , etc.; αἰσχροῖς γὰρ αἰσχρὰ πράγματ' ἐκδιδάσκεται S. El. 621 ; αἰσχρόν [ἐστι], c. inf., Il. 2.298 , S. Aj. 473 , etc.; αἰσχρόν, εἰ πύθοιτό τις ib. 1159 ; ἐν αἰσχρῷ θέσθαι τι E. Hec. 806 ; ἐπ' αἰσχροῖς on the ground of base actions, S. Fr. 188 , E. Hipp. 511 :—τὸ αἰ. as Subst., dishonour, S. Ph. 476 ; τὸ ἐμὸν αἰ. my disgrace, And. 2.9 ; τὸ καλὸν καὶ τὸ αἰ. virtue and vice, Arist. Rh. 1366a24 , etc. Adv., shamefully, S. El. 989 , Pl. Smp. 183d , etc.: Sup. αἴσχιστα A. Pr. 959 , S. OT 367 . ill-suited, αἰ. ὁ καιρός D. 18.178 ; αἰ. πρός τι awkward at it, X. Mem. 3.8.7 ; αἰσχρὸν καὶ ἄτεχνον Hp. Fract. 30 . Regul. Comp. and Sup. -ότερος, -ότατος are late, Phld. Rh. 2.58S. (prob.), Ath. 13.587b : elsewh. αἰσχίων, αἴσχιστος (formed from a Root αἰσχο-), Il. 21.437 , 2.216 ; double Sup. αἰσχιστότατος Olymp. in Alc. p.124 C. Adv., Sup. αἰσχίστως Mnasalc. ap. Ath. 4.163a , Man. 1.21 .
term_table.greek_sentence: κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ὁμότιμόν ἐστι φλεβοτομῆσαί τε τὸν ὑδεριῶντα καὶ κενῶσαι τινὶ τῶν ὑδραγωγῶν, εἶτα οὐκ αἰσχρὰ τὰ τοιαῦτα;
term_table.english_sentence_A: And in the same way it is equivalent to phlebotomize the dropsical patient and to evacuate him with one of the hydragogues. Then are such things not shameful?
term_table.english_sentence_B: In the same way it is all one to phlebotomise the dropsical patient and to evacuate him with one of the hydragogues. Then are not such things shameful?

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἀγαθός [αγ], ή, όν, Lacon. ἀγασός Ar. Lys. 1301 , Cypr. ἀζαθός GDI 57 :— good: of persons, well-born, gentle, opp. κακός, δειλός, οἷά τε τοῖς ἀγαθοῖσι παραδρώωσι χέρηες Od. 15.324 , cf. Il. 1.275 ; ἀφνειός τ' ἀ. τε Il. 13.664 , cf. Av. 1706 ; also, good things, dainties, Thgn. 1000 , Ar. Ach. 873 , etc.: good qualities, τοῖς ἀ., οἷς ἔχομεν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ Isoc. 8.32 , cf. term_table.greek_sentence: ὃ γὰρ εἴωθα λέγειν ἀεὶ, τοῦτο καὶ νῦν εἰπεῖν μοι καιρὸς, ἰδιώτης ἅπας τοῦ τοιούτου σοφιστοῦ κρείττων ἐστίν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For what I am always accustomed to say, this it is time for me to say now as well: every layman is better than such a sophist.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For what I am always accustomed to say, it is the right moment for me to say now too: every layman is better than a sophist of this sort.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: σοφισ-τής, οῦ, ὁ, master of one's craft, adept, expert, of diviners, Hdt. 2.49 ; of poets, μελέταν σοφισταῖς πρόσβαλον Pi. I. 5(4).28 , cf. Cratin. 2 ; of musicians, σοφιστὴς . . παραπαίων χέλυν A. Fr. 314 , cf. Eup. 447 , Pl.Com. 140 ; σοφιστῇ Θρῃκί (sc. Thamyris) E. Rh. 924 , cf. Ath. 14.632c : with modal words added, οἱ ς. τῶν ἱερῶν μελῶν Ael. NA 11.1 ; of the Creator of the universe (ὁ δημιουργός), πάνυ θαυμαστὸν λέγεις ς. Pl. R. 596d ; of cooks, εἰς τοὺς ς. τὸν μάγειρον ἐγγράφω Alex. 149.14 , cf. Euphro 1.11 ; οἱ τὴν ἱππείαν ς. skilled in . . , Ael. NA 13.9 : metaph., ς. πημάτων deviser, contriver of pains, E. Heracl. 993 :—then, wise, prudent or statesmanlike man, in which sense the seven Sages are called σοφισταί, Hdt. 1.29 , cf. Isoc. 15.235 , Arist. Fr. 5 , D. 61.50 ; of Pythagoras, Hdt. 4.95 ; of natural philosophers, Hp. VM 20 ; of Isocrates and Plato, D.H. Comp. 25 ; of the Βραχμᾶνες, Arr. An. 6.16.5 , cf. γυμνοσοφισταί; freq. with a slightly iron. sense, ἵνα μάθῃ ς. ὢν Διὸς νωθέστερος A. Pr. 62 , cf. 944 ; ψυχή . . κρείσσων σοφιστοῦ παντὸς εὑρέτις S. Fr. 101 , cf. E. Hipp. 921 : prov., μισῶ σοφιστὴν ὅτις οὐχ αὑτῷ σοφός Id. Fr. 905 : of the philosophic sage, Aristid. 2.311 J. from late v B.C., a Sophist, i.e. one who gave lessons in grammar, rhetoric, politics, mathematics, for money, such as Prodicus, Gorgias, Protagoras, τὴν σοφίαν τοὺς ἀργυρίου τῷ βουλομένῳ πωλοῦντας σοφιστὰς ἀποκαλοῦσιν X. Mem. 1.6.13 , cf. Cyn. 13.8 , Th. 3.38 , Pl. Prt. 31 3c , Euthd. 271c , La. 186c , Men. 85b , Isoc. 15.148 , Arist. SE 165a22 ; ς. ἄχρηστοι καὶ βίου δεόμενοι Lys. 33.3 ; but sts. even of Socrates (though he did not teach for money), Aeschin. 1.173 ; so of Christ, Luc. Peregr. 13 : hence (from the ill repute of the professed sophists at Athens), sophist (in bad sense), quibbler, cheat, Ar. Nu. 331 , 1111 , al., Pl. Sph. 268d ; γόητα καὶ σοφιστὴν ὀνομάζων D. 18.276 . later of the ῥήτορες, Professors of Rhetoric, and prose writers of the Empire, such as Philostratus and Libanius, Suid. ; Ἀπολλωνίδῃ σοφιστῇ PLips. 97 X 18 (iv A.D.); freq. as a title in epitaphs, IG 3.625 , 637 , 680 , 775 , 14.935 .
term_table.greek_sentence: εἰ γὰρ καὶ [340] μηδὲν ἄλλο, τὰς γοῦν κατὰ φύσιν ἐννοίας οἱ ἰδιῶται διασώζουσιν, ἀπολλύντων καὶ ταύτας διὰ μοχθηροὺς ἐθισμοὺς τῶν σοφιστῶν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For if [340] nothing else, the laymen at any rate preserve the natural notions, whereas the sophists destroy even these through bad habits of training.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For even if [340] nothing else, laymen at least preserve the natural notions, whereas the sophists destroy even these through bad habituations.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἔναγχος, Adv. just now, lately, Ar. Nu. 639 , Eup. 181.2 , Lys. 19.50 , Pl. Grg. 462c , D. 21.36 ; τὸ ἔ. Ar. Ec. 823 ; opp. πάλαι, Isoc. 19.43 ; τὸ ἔ. πάθος the recent misfortune, App. BC 1.9 : c. gen., ἔ. τοῦ Χρόνου D.H. 7.45 .
term_table.greek_sentence: ἔναγχος γοῦν τις ἰδιώτης οὐκ ἄφρων ἐξανθημάτων αὐτῷ κατὰ πολλὰ μόρια τοῦ σώματος ἐξαίφνης γενομένων ἑλκωδῶν τε καὶ κακοχρόων ἧκεν ὡς τὸν ἰατρὸν, ἀξιῶν ὅτι τάχιστα καθαρθῆναι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Recently, at any rate, a certain layman, not a foolish one, when eruptions, ulcerous and of bad colour, had suddenly arisen on many parts of his body, came to the physician, demanding to be purged as quickly as possible.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Recently, at any rate, a layman who was not unintelligent, when ulcerous and discoloured eruptions had suddenly appeared on him over many parts of the body, came to the physician, asking to be purged as quickly as possible.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἔννοια, ἡ, (νοῦς) act of thinking, reflection, cogitation ( συντονία διανοίας Pl. Def. 414a ); ἄξιον ἐννοίας Id. Lg. 657a ,al. notion, conception, χρόνου ἔννοια Id. Ti. 47a ; ἐν ταῖς περὶ τὸ ὂν . . ἐννοίαις Id. Phlb. 59d ; ἔ. λαβεῖν to form an idea, opp. αἴσθησιν λαβεῖν, Id. Phd. 73c ; τοῦ καλοῦ ἔ. ἔχειν Arist. EN 1179b15 ; ἐννοίας χάριν λέγειν Id. Rhet., thought, opp. diction (λέξις), Hermog. Id. 2.4 , cf. Prog. 6 .
term_table.greek_sentence: ἀλλ’ οἱ πάντα μᾶλλον ἢ τὸν Ἱπποκράτειον λόγον ἀληθεύειν βουλόμενοι καὶ τὰς κοινὰς ἐννοίας προσαπολλύουσι τῇ φιλονεικίᾳ.
term_table.english_sentence_A: When the physician ordered him rather to be phlebotomized, 'Are you not mad?' he said, 'for it stands to reason that the good will be evacuated together with the corrupted.' But those who want anything whatever to be true rather than the Hippocratic account lose, in addition, even the common notions through their contentiousness.
term_table.english_sentence_B: And when the physician instead bade him be bled, 'Do not be mad,' he said, 'for it stands to reason that together with what is corrupted, what is good is evacuated as well.' But those who would rather anything be true than the Hippocratic account destroy the common notions too, through their love of contention.

term_table.greek_sentence: κᾄπειτ’ ἐπιπηδῶσι μὲν ἡμῖν ὡς διασπασόμενοι, τοῖς δὲ ἐπ’ αὐτῶν τῶν ἔργων ἐλέγχοις ἄχθονται.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And then they leap upon us as though they would tear us to pieces, yet they are vexed at the refutations drawn from the facts themselves.
term_table.english_sentence_B: And then they leap upon us as if to tear us apart, yet are vexed by the refutations drawn from the works themselves.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἀκούσας γοῦν τις τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς τοιαύτης ἐμπληξίας ἰατρῶν, ὡς ἐγὼ παμπόλλους ἐθεράπευσα μόνῃ καθάρσει.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: καρκιν-ώδης, ες, = καρκινοειδής , Arist. PA 683b31 , Plu. 2.980b . cancerous, Dsc. Eup. 2.72 , Ruf. ap. Orib. 45.11.1 ; ὄγκος Gal. 18(1).80 , Alex.Aphr. Pr. 1.92 .
term_table.greek_sentence: καί τις ἄλλος ὅτι καρκινώδεις διαθέσεις ἀρχομένας, τούς τε καλουμένους ἐλέφαντας καὶ φαγεδαίνας, ἄλλα τε πολλὰ τῶν κακοήθων ἑλκῶν ὁμοίως ἐμίσησεν, ἄλλος δὲ ὅτι σκοτωματικοὺς ἐθεράπευσα καθάρσεσι μόναις, ἄλλος δ’ ὅτι μανιώδεις ἐπιλήπτους τε καὶ μελαγχολικοὺς, ἔτι δὲ καὶ κεφαλαίᾳ κάμνοντας οὐκ ὀλίγους ἐξιασάμην καθάρσεσι μόναις, ὥσπερ γε καὶ ἰσχιαδικούς.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And another likewise hated me because I treated incipient cancerous conditions, the so-called elephas and phagedaenae, and many other malignant ulcers; another because I treated scotomatic patients by purgations alone; another because I completely cured maniacal, epileptic and melancholic patients, and moreover not a few suffering from cephalaea, by purgations alone, just as I did sciatic patients too.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Another likewise hated me because [I had treated] incipient cancerous conditions, the so-called elephantes and phagedainai, and many other malignant ulcers. Another, because I treated those subject to skotōma by purgations alone.

term_table.greek_sentence: οὕτω δὲ καὶ ἀλγήματα χρόνια κατὰ πολλοὺς τόπους ἐσπαρμένα καὶ τοῦτον δὴ τὸν ἔναγχος ὡς κωλικὸν ἤδη τριῶν μηνῶν ὑπὸ τῶν ἰατρῶν θεραπευσάμενον, ἐπὶ τὸ χεῖρον προϊόντα, πάντα ἀποῤῥῖψαι κελεύσας ἐκεῖνα καθάρσεσι μόναις ἰασάμην.
term_table.english_sentence_A: So too chronic pains scattered over many places, and indeed that man recently who had already been treated for three months by the physicians as a colic patient and was progressing toward the worse — having ordered him to throw away all those remedies, I cured him by purgations alone.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Another, because I cured by purgations alone maniacal, epileptic and melancholic patients, and also not a few suffering from kephalaia, as well as sufferers from sciatica. In the same way I cured by purgations alone chronic pains scattered over many places.

term_table.greek_sentence: δι’ ὅλης ἡμέρας ἔχω καὶ ἄλλα [342] λέγειν ἔργα θαυμάσια καθάρσεσιν ἑπόμενα, περὶ ὧν ἀγνοεῖν εἰκός ἐστι τοὺς μηδέποτε τὴν περὶ τὰ καθαίροντα φάρμακα τέχνην μεμαθηκότας.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For a whole day I could go on recounting still other [342] marvellous effects that follow upon purgings, of which it is natural that those who have never learned the art concerning purgative drugs should be ignorant.

Ant. 426 ; of a horse which has thrown its rider, AP 13.18 (Parmeno). c. gen., bare of, separated from, ψ. σώματος οὖσα [ἡ ψυχή] Pl. Lg. 899a ; τέχναι ψ. τῶν πράξεων Id. Plt. 258d ; ψ. ὅπλων Id. Lg. 834c ; ἱππέων X. Cyr. 5.3.57 ; θηρία μεμονωμένα καὶ ψ. τῶν Ἰνδῶν Plb. 11.1.12 . stripped of appendages, naked, ψ. [τρόπις] the bare keel with the planks torn from it, Od. 12.421 ; ψ. μάχαιραι swords alone, without other arms, etc., X. Cyr. 4.5.58 ; θάλαττα ψ. blank sea, Aristid. Or. 25(43).50 . freq. in Prose, as a military term, of soldiers without heavy armour, light troops, such as archers and slingers, opp. ὁπλῖται, first in Hdt. 7.158 , al., freq. in Th. , e. g. ὁπλίζει τὸν δῆμον, πρότερον ψ. ὄντα 3.27 , cf. Arr. Tact. 3.3 ; ὁ ψ. ὅμιλος Th. 4.125 ; so ψιλοί or τὸ ψιλόν, opp. τὸ ὁπλιτικόν, X. HG 4.2.17 , Arist. Pol. 1321a7 ; ψιλός, opp. ὡπλισμένος, S. Aj. 1123 : coupled with ἄσκευος, Id. OC 1029 ; ψιλὸς στρατεύσομαι Ar. Th. 232 ; ψ. δύναμις Arist. Pol. 1321a13 ; αἱ κοῦφαι καὶ αἱ ψ. ἐργασίαι work that belongs to unarmed soldiers, ib. 1321a25 ; ψ. χερσὶν πρὸς καθωπλισμένους Ael. VH 6.2 : but ψ. ἔχων τὴν κεφαλήν bare-headed, without helmet, X. An. 1.8.6 ; ψ. ἵππος a horse without housings, Id. Eq. 7.5 : unarmed, defenceless, S. Ph. 953 . λόγος ψ. bare language, i. e. prose, opp. to poetry which is clothed in the garb of metre, Pl. Mx. 239c , Phld. Mus. p.97K. ; more freq. in pl., ψ. λόγοι Pl. Lg. 669d ; opp. τὰ μέτρα, Arist. Rh. 1404b14 , 33 : but in D. 27.54 ψ. λόγος is a mere speech, a speech unsupported by evidence; and in Pl. Tht. 165a ψιλοὶ λόγοι are mere forms of argumentation, dialectical abstractions (so ψιλῶς λέγειν speak nakedly, without alleging proofs, Id. Phdr. 262c , cf. Lg. 811e ); τὰς πράξεις αὐτὰς ψιλὰς φράζοντες Arist. Rh.Al. 1438b27 . ποίησις ψ. mere poetry, without music, i. e. Epic poetry, opp. Lyric (ἡ ἐν ᾠδῇ), Pl. Phdr. 278c ; so ἄνευ ὀργάνων ψ. λόγοι Id. Pr. 922a16 ; ἡ ψ. φωνή the ordinary sound of the voice, opp. singing (ἡ ᾠδική), D.H. Comp. 11 . ψ. μουσική instrumental music unaccompanied by the voice, opp. ἡ μετὰ μελῳδίας, Arist. Pol. 1339b20 ; ψιλῷ μέλει διαγωνίζεσθαι πρὸς ᾠδὴν καὶ κιθάραν, of Marsyas, Plu. 2.713d , cf. Phld. Mus. p.100K. ; so ψ. κιθάρισις καὶ αὔλησις Pl. Lg. 669e ; ψιλὸς αὐλητής one who plays unaccompanied on the flute (cf. ψιλοκιθαριστής), Phryn. 145 . mere, simple (cf. supr. IV. 1 ), ἀριθμητικὴ ψιλή, opp. geometry and the like , Pl. Plt. 299e ; ὕδωρ ψ., opp. σὺν οἴνῳ, Hp. Int. 35 ; ψ. ἀναίρεσις mere removal, Phld. Sign. 12 ; ψ. ἄνδρες, i. e. men without women, Antip.Stoic. 3.254 :—Oedipus calls Antigone his ψιλὸν ὄμμα, as being the one poor eye left him, S. OC 866 . Adv. ψιλῶς merely, only, Plu. Per. 15 ; ἕνεκα τοῦ ψ. εἰπεῖν for the purpose of merely saying, Sch. Il. Oxy. 1086.65 ; ψ. ὀνομάζειν call by the bare name (without epithet), Phld. Vit. p.39J. A.translation: [323] GALEN, ON THE POWER OF PURGATIVE DRUGS. The most ancient of the physicians seem to have left bad opinions unrefuted for the same reason for which the most ancient of the lawgivers also left the greatest of wrongdoings unpunished. For since at that time vice was more moderate, and men neither attempted the greatest injustices nor brought themselves to act shamelessly in the most obvious matters, how could anyone either have fixed a punishment for things that had not happened at all, or have brought a refutation against things that no one had said at all?

But since, as wickedness increased over time, there was no longer anything either undared or [324] unsaid among human beings, the lawgivers devised many new modes of punishment for wrongdoers, while those who honour truth devised manifold forms of refutation against the sophists — which is what we too now seem likely to do, refuting those who abolish the attractive power of purgative drugs over the humours which they evacuate, and assert that they possess a certain transformative power over all things alike that come into contact with them. Nothing, however, has been said by Hippocrates against such an opinion. For in his time there was not yet either Asclepiades, who was openly shameless and stripped, as it were, for some prize (ἔπαθλόν τινα) against the truth, or Erasistratus, who, with a certain modesty indeed, nonetheless overturned the whole chief point itself, that which manifestly holds concerning purgative drugs. For indeed the most active and most proper power of nature, the attractive power, Erasistratus knows nowhere in his own writings, but rather employs in its place the following toward what is being emptied.

And the power in purgative drugs is a part of the power that attracts what is proper to it, [325] just as is also that by which the bile is separated off, and the urine, and many other things that are brought about by nature in the health of animals, and in the cures of diseases and in the diseases themselves, both by physicians and, not least, by nature itself. Since, then, Hippocrates said nothing against those who abolish attraction from among the things that exist, because the doctrine did not yet have so brazen a champion as many of those after them became, it would be just for us to contend for the truth in Hippocrates' place, and first to recall what sort of thing these men say, and then next to show that they do not speak correctly. Their argument, then, is as follows. The purgative drug alters whatever humour it touches into its own form: the one they name cholagogue producing yellow bile, just as the one they call phlegmagogue produces phlegm; the one they call hydragogue bringing about a kind of watery nature; and yet another rendering whatever humour it touches black bile.

[326] To put it briefly, what is called purgation is, according to their account, a change and alteration of all the humours in the veins, not an evacuation of one of them. But if this is what you want, let us now say to them that whether someone takes a drug that draws bile, or phlegm, or black bile, or serous moisture, all the humours from the veins are evacuated. And indeed, purging someone with such a drug would then differ in this respect only from evacuating the blood by cutting a vein, inasmuch as in phlebotomies it is excreted such as it was present before, whereas in purgations it is altered not only in colour but also in consistency. For the drug that draws watery humours makes everything in the veins fluid and thin, even if it happened to be very thick before; while that which draws black bile, conversely, makes everything thick and stagnant, even if before it was very fluid. And accordingly, our choice between phlebotomizing and purging will be made according to certain other indications, but will not be made according to the very kind of the things evacuated. And what are these other indications?

Many [327] are readier for phlebotomy than others, some for purgation, just as there are also others who would sooner suffer anything whatever than be phlebotomized. And some endure having some part of the body cut off rather than swallowing a drug. And indeed some have their stomach upset by purging drugs, while others take them without distress. On the basis of such indications, then, we shall phlebotomize some people and give others the purging drug—not on the basis of those which the Asclepiadae held, who believe that phlebotomy evacuates all the humors in the veins equally, whereas purgation does not do so equally, but evacuates one single humor and that one alone, of which the drug is said to be the evacuant. For this reason they also say that the blood is purged by such drugs, not evacuated as in phlebotomies. These things follow from your hypotheses, whether you will it or not. But I shall recall their main points.

According to the Asclepiadeans, the evacuation in phlebotomies is equal for all the humours in the veins, whereas [328] that in purgations is not equal, but is a removal of the others, so as to render the blood pure. According to Erasistratus and his followers, the evacuation of all the humours is equal, as in phlebotomies, so also in purgations, which they will say are not really purgations at all, but evacuations accompanied by corruption and alteration of what is being evacuated. So let the sophists, both the moderately shameless and the utterly shameless, come to the contest and compete against me, as in a stadium, not with arguments nor with long drivel, but with the very deeds to which I summon them in this most populous city, in which countless jaundiced persons can be found every day, and countless dropsical ones. For it is enough for me to make my argument first about these. Let someone bring me one of these, without fever, having his whole body full of bitter bile, and let him observe how, after preparing the man for some days, when the right moment already seems to me to have come, by giving one of the bile-drawing laxatives (ὑπήλατον), I bring the man back to his natural state by means of such a purgation, without undertaking anything further at all with regard to the body.

[329] But this we have demonstrated not once or twice, but very many times, to the half-wicked among them, and many we have converted to better views. Not, however, on this account, sophist, do I bid you trust those who bear witness, but rather, whenever you wish, to observe for yourself the jaundiced man recovering his natural colour by a single purgation. When, then, you see this happening, noble sir, you may dare, taking your stand in the midst, with a brilliant voice—raising it, at any rate, after the fashion of a herald—to stretch out a long discourse, such as you often deliver to your pupils, to the effect that what is proper to it is not drawn by each of the purgatives, but that everything contained in the veins, of whatever sort it may be, is changed into that into which the power of the drug has the nature to alter it; and that now this man who has been treated for the jaundice has benefited not by the humour's being evacuated, but by the common principle of evacuation. "Observe, at any rate, how I shall benefit in like manner another of those in such a condition, either by phlebotomizing him or by giving some other of the laxatives."

Having said this, next, for my benefit, take two jaundiced patients: phlebotomize the one, and evacuate the other by means of one of such [330] purgatives as all men are persuaded evacuate black bile, while you are persuaded that it does not evacuate it but generates it. And then, if you benefit him, rendering his body of good colour, I shall concede to you whatever you may wish me to suffer; but if you benefit the man not at all, but rather bring him to the extreme of harm, change over to the better and emulate the art of Hippocrates. But enough concerning the jaundiced. Passing on to the dropsical patient, observe again that this man too is not affected in the same way by phlebotomy and by one of the hydragogue drugs. For if I should fail to show the watery matter in the lower belly being evacuated by a drug, then it is open to you to condemn the ancient doctrine, which holds that such a humour is not generated, as you say, but is drawn out of the body by the drug, and to do against us whatever you wish. And yet, if you were to give a drug that draws out black bile or yellow bile, you will not empty the swelling; and thus each of the drugs is attractive of some humour proper to it.

But you, if you think that all are altered alike [331] and that what happens is a common evacuation, not a purgation, are free to cut the vein. If someone living among the Indians were writing these things and issuing this challenge, it would be difficult to refute him. But since he is a man seen by us every day, and is being summoned to the very refutation by means of deeds, I do not know how you are not ashamed, talking such nonsense. I am not going to say that I have cleansed the body of very many jaundiced patients of the bilious humour by a single purgation; for indeed countless people bear witness to this. But if the most shameless sophists are going to pretend to disbelieve all men, let them themselves watch the very deed taking place, as often as they wish. And yet why do I say "let them watch"? For I have already demonstrated this to them many times, and I even recall a certain man taking refuge in some such idle talk. For he said that it is not some one kind of humour that is drawn by each of the drugs, but that each of them simply draws, like the things that suck (βδάλλοντα); and that what is thinner among the humours follows the attraction first, next after it the thicker, and then in this way the thickest.

[332] Of those drugs, then, whose strength is exhausted more quickly, the evacuation stops at the watery humours; but of those whose strength holds out longer, by these the yellow bile too is evacuated; and those which are strongest draw out the black bile as well. On the spot, then, this fellow seemed to his devotees to be speaking well, and they all shouted applause for him, and at a great run he left us and departed, knowing for certain, I think, that if he stayed he would be refuted. However, when on the following day a certain book was given by us to his chorus-members, in which there was a refutation of what had thus suddenly been ventured, he was never again persuasive in the same way to those very people, being at a loss to resolve the objections put forward. For the following had been written in the book: "Yesterday you ran away from the argument, doing something like a contestant who snatches the crown and flees before competing; but today you will not escape refutation. For this book will follow you, having fallen into the hands of the chorus-members around you.

For the argument is no less addressed to them than to you—to men who had never before heard you concede that there exists [333] attraction in any existing thing at all, but who yesterday heard you admit that everything contained in the veins is drawn in common by the drug. For it would have been right for them not merely not to admire, or to praise at all, what was said, but to regard it as a betrayal of the positions he laid down from the beginning. For concerning the separation of urine and of yellow bile and black, and many other activities in the body, you produce a great many arguments on every occasion, conceding anything rather than that attraction of what is proper to itself is a certain natural activity belonging to each body; but now you have conceded not only that attraction exists, but even attraction of absolutely everything—which is a far greater admission than to speak of attraction of what is proper. For that, just as there is in animals a certain power expulsive of what is alien, so there is also a certain power attractive of what is proper to each existing thing, seems reasonable to all men—at least to those who are not yet wise with our wisdom; but that all things are drawn alike by something, whether they happen to be akin in their qualities or most contrary, is full of astonishing unreason.

Thus you have not only conceded attraction, but also, [334] far worse than you ought, you have said that it is an attraction not only of the things proper to each, but simply of all things. In this way, then, you seem to me to deserve not so much to be praised as to be drunkenly abused by the members of your chorus. And that you have never even used purgative drugs, but are a layman and destitute of medical practice, this too I think I shall demonstrate quickly. All drugs that are of such a nature as to purge black bile evacuate black bile immediately from the beginning. The evacuations differ from one another in that the first are more fluid, while those that follow them are always progressively thicker. This very same thing holds also for the drugs that purge out phlegm and for those that purge out yellow bile. For each of them draws from the beginning its own proper humour, but in the course of time a thicker one; it is not, however, as you suppose, that someone first filled a whole basin with serous residue, then next another with yellow bile, and then another with phlegm, and then in this way the black bile is evacuated. From this it is clear that what is proper to the drug is drawn by it, while the watery part that floats on the surface accompanies it.

But it is possible for you to observe this now, even if you did not before: that people evacuate a very great quantity of watery and bilious matter [335] upon such doses of drugs, whereas the total evacuation that occurs in them upon the evacuants of black bile is the very least. Yet, on your hypothesis at least, the total amount should always be greatest upon the evacuants of black bile, and least upon the watery and bilious ones. For your argument, I suppose, distinguished the kind of the matters evacuated by the weakness and strength of the drugs, as in the case of the evacuants of black bile. But since these differ from the others in strength, the evacuation will be exceedingly great: first of all the watery matter in its entirety, then of the bilious, then of the phlegmatic, then of black bile itself. Whereas with the weak laxatives only the watery matters themselves will be evacuated. But none of these things is seen to happen, so that these phenomena overthrow your argument. It is also worth your answering why, when the thicker matters are always evacuated after the thinner, black bile is drawn out before the blood, although it is, as it were, a kind of sediment of the blood, as the lees are in wines.

[336] Perhaps, then, you will inquire whether there is any drug that draws out blood straightaway from the very beginning. There is, my excellent friend, but no one would use it. Why? you will perhaps say. Because this would be to slaughter the man, not to purge him. For purgatives are called purgatives by everyone for this very reason, that they render the blood clean of the aforementioned residues. Yet there is no physician so wise as to wish to evacuate all the blood and to leave the other humours behind in the body. Hence they reckon among the deleterious poisons all such drugs as produce an evacuation of blood through the veins in the stomach and the intestines. But according to your hypothesis not even these ought to evacuate blood from the beginning. As for the names of such drugs, even if I knew them with certainty, I would not disclose them in writing. But this alone it is safe for me to relate: what happened among the Thracian Bithynians when we were still children. A certain man found a herb of such a kind that whoever took some of it excreted blood and so perished.

Since many, then, were dying in a similar [337] manner, they deemed what was happening worthy of a more exact inquiry, and they found the poisoner and brought him before the governor of the people. And when that man made it his business not only to put the fellow himself to death but also to find out whether anyone else had either taught him or learned from him, he said that he had learned the herb from no one, but that once, while carrying a pig's liver to a certain suburb, when his belly had become fixed (πηξάσης τῆς γαστρός), he set it down upon a plant, and then, on taking it up again, saw bloody ichors flowing out of the whole liver onto the plant; and that from this he conjectured that it was likely the plant draws blood, and gave it, for the sake of a trial, to one of the people he happened upon, and when he found what he had hoped, he used it thereafter for evil. Nor, he said, had he shown the plant to any other human being. These things that poisoner said while being tortured at great length. And the governor of the people, since in the account which he gave concerning the plant he said that it grew in very great abundance everywhere, ordered him to be led away to be put to death with his eyes bound, so that he might not show it to anyone on the way.

So that, my good friend, it is likely that many drugs have been discovered which possess such a [338] power as to draw blood straight away from the outset. But it is reasonable that they be kept in silence, just as the other poisons are kept in silence by all who have sense. For there have already been some who were ungrudging even in the teaching of these things, displaying a kind of monstrous liberality and writing down the preparations of each of the poisons; but such men are not among those who have sense, just as neither are you, if you ask us which of the drugs are evacuant of blood. Let us therefore bring the argument back again to its original aim. He who says that all the humours are drawn equally, but that the most free-flowing are separated off first and the others in succession, betrays his dearest tenets, by admitting that the attractive power exists among the things that are. It is concerning this power that his chorus behaves shamelessly, and has brought itself to say outlandish things about the separation of bile and of urine, about distribution (anadosis) and other such matters, and moreover it posits things contrary to the phenomena, as we showed before.

For if this hypothesis is true, the total evacuation will be greatest with the drugs that draw black bile, and least with those that draw the serous [339] residues. And yet I shall show you ten thousand times, sophist, if you are willing, now at any rate if never before, to look at the works of the art, that a very great evacuation always follows the hydragogue drugs, and a very small one follows those that purge out black bile. And I shall show, too, that black bile is evacuated right at the beginning. So the one who says that all the humours are drawn alike is to this degree insensible and ignorant; and let the one who says that they are altered consider in turn to what extent, on his account, it will make no difference whether one phlebotomizes the jaundiced patient or purges him with a cholagogue drug. And in the same way it is equivalent to phlebotomize the dropsical patient and to evacuate him with one of the hydragogues. Then are such things not shameful? The many, hearing such things when the physicians contradict one another, laugh—not rightly—and they have all condemned reasoning, and they call those who utter anything at all "word-physicians" (logiatroi). For what I am always accustomed to say, this it is time for me to say now as well: every layman is better than such a sophist.

For if [340] nothing else, the laymen at any rate preserve the natural notions, whereas the sophists destroy even these through bad habits of training. Recently, at any rate, a certain layman, not a foolish one, when eruptions, ulcerous and of bad colour, had suddenly arisen on many parts of his body, came to the physician, demanding to be purged as quickly as possible. When the physician ordered him rather to be phlebotomized, 'Are you not mad?' he said, 'for it stands to reason that the good will be evacuated together with the corrupted.' But those who want anything whatever to be true rather than the Hippocratic account lose, in addition, even the common notions through their contentiousness. And then they leap upon us as though they would tear us to pieces, yet they are vexed at the refutations drawn from the facts themselves. It would be just that, as we put up with them when they abuse Hippocrates over matters of which they are ignorant, and attempt to persuade them, so they too should endure the refutations, and best of all, if possible, be fond of those who taught them; but if not, at least not hate them altogether. At any rate, one of the physicians belonging to this sort of stupidity, having heard that I had treated very many by purgation alone

— of those, namely, who have the so-called [341] alopecias — from that point began to hate me. And another likewise hated me because I treated incipient cancerous conditions, the so-called elephas and phagedaenae, and many other malignant ulcers; another because I treated scotomatic patients by purgations alone; another because I completely cured maniacal, epileptic and melancholic patients, and moreover not a few suffering from cephalaea, by purgations alone, just as I did sciatic patients too. So too chronic pains scattered over many places, and indeed that man recently who had already been treated for three months by the physicians as a colic patient and was progressing toward the worse — having ordered him to throw away all those remedies, I cured him by purgations alone. I also cured a female flux, in a certain not inconspicuous one of the women at Rome, by purgations alone, as indeed also in many other more obscure women both this very same affection and certain others of those that arise in the womb. And as for erysipelata, what need is there even to say that there is no more effective remedy than a bile-drawing drug, just as the phlegm-drawing drug is most contrary to them.

For a whole day I could go on recounting still other [342] marvellous effects that follow upon purgings, of which it is natural that those who have never learned the art concerning purgative drugs should be ignorant. For where they do not even think that there exists any purgative drug at all, how indeed will they know in which cases one must use it, or in what manner? For this reason some treat the affections guided by bare and sole experience; but these wise men of ours, who take reason too in hand, not so as to add anything to what has been discovered through experience, but so as to overturn even this, practise medicine far worse than those who set out from bare and sole irrational routines. Of all these things there is one origin and source, the hatred toward Hippocrates, from which source there have flowed many other things, and also this very inquiry now before us, that concerning the attractive power, of which the power of purgative drugs is a part, or a species, or whatever one might wish to call it.

B.translation: [323] GALEN, ON THE POWER OF PURGATIVE DRUGS. It seems that the most ancient of the physicians left pernicious opinions unrefuted for the same reason that the most ancient of the lawgivers also left the greatest offences unpunished. For since vice was more moderate in that time, and people neither undertook to commit the greatest wrongs nor brought themselves to the most flagrant shamelessness, how could anyone either have prescribed a punishment for things that had never happened at all, or have brought a refutation against things that no one had said at all?

But since, as vice grew over time, nothing was any longer either undared or unsaid among [324] men, the lawgivers devise many new kinds of punishment for wrongdoers, and those who honour truth devise many-sided forms of refutation against the sophists. This is what we too, it seems, would now do, refuting those who abolish the attractive faculty of purgative drugs for the humours that they evacuate, and who claim instead that these drugs have a certain transformative faculty over everything that comes near them, all alike. Nothing was said by Hippocrates against such an opinion. For in his time there was not yet either Asclepiades, who openly behaved shamelessly and stripped, as if for some prize, to contend against the truth, or Erasistratus, who acted with a certain modesty but overturned the whole main point itself, which manifestly holds concerning purgative drugs. For Erasistratus nowhere in his own writings recognises the attractive faculty, the most active and most proper faculty of nature, but rather uses in its place the following toward what is being emptied.

The power in purgative drugs is a part of the power that attracts what is proper [325] to each thing, just as is also the power by which bile is separated off, and urine, and many other things that are brought about by nature both in the health of animals and in the cures of diseases and in the diseases themselves, by physicians and, not least, by nature itself. Since, then, Hippocrates said nothing against those who abolish attraction from among the things that exist, because the doctrine had not yet found a champion as reckless as many of those after them turned out to be, it would be just for us to contend for the truth in place of Hippocrates: first to recall what sort of thing these men say, and then next to show that they do not speak correctly. Their argument, then, is as follows. The purgative drug alters whatever humour it touches into its own particular form. One produces yellow bile, which they call cholagogue; another, likewise, produces phlegm, which they call phlegmagogue; another renders a certain watery nature, which they call hydragogue; and another makes black bile out of whatever humour it touches.

[326] To put it briefly, what is called purgation is, according to their argument, a change and alteration of all the humours in the veins, not an evacuation of one of them. But if this is what you would have, let us now say to them that, whether someone takes a drug that draws bile, or phlegm, or black [bile], or serous fluid, all the humours are evacuated from the veins. And indeed, then, purging someone with such a drug differs from evacuating the blood by cutting a vein only in this respect: in phlebotomies it is excreted just as it was present beforehand, whereas in purgations it has been changed not only in colour but also in consistency. For the drug that draws watery [humours] makes everything in the veins fluid and thin, even if it happened previously to be very thick; that which draws black [bile], conversely, makes everything thick and stagnant, even if it was before very fluid. And accordingly our choice between phlebotomizing and purging will be made according to certain other aims, but it will not be made according to the very kind of the things evacuated. What, then, are the other aims?

Many [327] are readier for venesection than others are, some for purgation, just as others, again, would sooner suffer anything whatever than be venesected. Some would rather submit to having some part of the body cut off than swallow a drug. And indeed some have their stomach upset by purgative drugs, while others take them without distress. From such considerations, then, we shall venesect some people and give the purgative drug to others. We shall not proceed from the considerations the Asclepiadeans held. They believed that venesection evacuates all the humours in the veins equally, but that purgation does not do so equally: it evacuates some single humour, and that one alone, which the drug is said to draw off. For this reason they also say that the blood is purged by such drugs, not emptied as in venesections. These things follow from your hypotheses, whether you are willing or unwilling. I shall remind them of the main heads of these points.

According to the Asclepiads, the evacuation in phlebotomies is equal for all the humours in the veins, but [328] that in purgations is not equal; it is rather a removal of the others, so as to render the blood pure. According to Erasistratus and his followers, the evacuation of all is equal, in purgations just as in phlebotomies, and they will say that these are not really purgations at all, but evacuations together with corruption and alteration of what is evacuated. Now that we have come to the contest, let both the moderately shameless among the sophists and the utterly shameless compete, as in a stadium, not against me with words or with long drivel, but with the deeds themselves. To these I challenge them, here in this most populous city, in which countless jaundiced persons can be found every day, and countless dropsical ones. For it is enough for me to make my argument first about these. Let someone bring me one of these people, without fever, whose whole body is full of bitter bile, and let him watch how I prepare the man for some days, and then, when it seems to me to be the right moment, give him some evacuant from among the bile-drawing drugs, and by such a purgation bring the man back to his natural state, without doing anything further at all to his body.

[329] But this we have demonstrated not once or twice but very many times to the half-depraved among them, and we have brought many of them over to the better view. Not, however, on this account, sophist, do I bid you trust those who bear witness to it; rather, I bid you see for yourself, whenever you wish, the jaundiced patient recovering his natural colour with a single purgation. When, then, you see this happening, my noble friend, dare to take your stand in the midst and with a ringing voice, raising it, indeed, in the manner of a herald, to draw out a long speech, such as you often deliver to your pupils: that it is not what is proper to each that is drawn by each of the purging drugs, but that everything contained in the veins, of whatever kind it may be, is changed into whatever the power of the drug has the nature to alter it into. 'And now this man who has been treated for jaundice was benefited not by the evacuation of the humour, but by the common principle of evacuation. Watch, then, how I shall benefit equally another of those so affected, either by phlebotomizing him or by giving some other of the downward purgatives.'

Having said this, take for me next two of those suffering from jaundice: bleed the one, and evacuate the other by means of one of those [330] laxatives which all men are persuaded evacuates black bile, but which you are persuaded does not evacuate it but generates it. And then, if you benefit him, rendering his body of good colour, I shall grant you that I suffer whatever you may wish; but if you have not benefited the man at all, and have instead brought him to the extreme of harm, change over to the better and emulate the art of Hippocrates. But enough about those suffering from jaundice. Passing to the dropsical patient, observe again that he too is not affected in the same way by venesection and by one of the hydragogue drugs. For if I should fail to show the watery fluid in the lower belly being evacuated by the drug, then you may condemn the ancient doctrine, which holds that such a humour is not generated, as you say, but is drawn out of the body by the drug; and do against us whatever you wish. And indeed, if you give a drug that draws off black or yellow bile, you will not empty the swelling; and thus each of the drugs is attractive of some humour proper to it.

But if you think that all are altered alike [331] and that what takes place is a common evacuation, not a purgation, you are free to cut the vein. Now if someone living among the Indians issued this challenge in writing, it would be difficult to refute him. But since he is a man who is seen by us every day, and who is summoned to the very refutation that comes through the actual work, I do not know how you are not ashamed of talking nonsense. I am not going to say that I have purged the body of a great many jaundiced persons of the bilious humour by a single purgation, for countless people bear witness to this. But if the most shameless sophists are going to pretend to disbelieve all men, let them themselves watch the work itself being done, as often as they wish. And yet why do I say 'let them watch'? For I have already demonstrated this to them many times, and indeed I remember someone even laying hold of some such idle chatter as this. For he said that it is not some one kind of humour that is drawn by each of the drugs, but that each of them simply draws, like things that suck, and that the drawing is followed first by what is thinner among the humours, next after it by what is thicker, and then in this way by what is thickest.

[332] Of those drugs, then, whose strength is dissipated more quickly, the evacuation stops at the watery humours; of those whose strength holds out longer, yellow bile too is evacuated; and those that are strongest draw out black bile as well. At the time, then, this fellow seemed to the members of his coterie to speak well, and they all shouted their acclaim of him, and he took himself off, leaving us behind at a great run, knowing for certain, I think, that if he stayed he would be refuted. But when, on the following day, we gave his chorus a certain book containing a refutation of what had been so rashly ventured on the spur of the moment, he was never again as persuasive as before, even to those very people, since he was at a loss to resolve the objections put to him. For this is what had been written in the book: 'Yesterday you ran away from the argument, doing something like a competitor who snatches the crown and flees before competing; but today you will not escape refutation. For this book will follow you, having fallen into the hands of the chorus around you.'

For the argument is addressed no less to them than to you: to those who had never before heard you concede that attraction exists [333] in anything whatsoever, but yesterday heard you agreeing that all the contents of the veins alike are attracted by the drug. For it would have been right for them, far from admiring or in any way praising what was said, to regard it as a betrayal of what he had laid down from the beginning. For on every occasion you people hold a great many discourses about the separation of urine, and of yellow and black bile, and about many other activities in the body, conceding anything rather than that attraction is a natural activity belonging to each body with respect to what is proper to it. But now you have conceded not only that attraction exists, but that it is of all things without qualification, which is a far greater admission than to say 'of what is proper.' For that, just as there is in animals a certain faculty that excretes what is alien, so there is also in each of the things that exist one that attracts what is proper, seems reasonable to all men, at least to those not yet wise with our wisdom. But that all things are attracted equally by something, whether they happen to be akin in their qualities or most contrary, is full of astonishing irrationality.

Thus you have not only conceded attraction, but have also, [334] far worse than you ought, declared it to be not only of what is proper but simply of all things. So it seems to me that you deserve not to be praised so much as to be drunkenly abused by the chorus about you. That you have never even used purgative drugs, but are a layman and without resource in the works of medicine, this too I think I shall demonstrate quickly. Whatever is naturally disposed to purge black bile evacuates black bile straightaway from the beginning. The evacuations differ from one another in that the first are more fluid, while those following them are always progressively thicker. This very thing holds also for those that purge out phlegm and yellow bile. For each of them attracts its proper humour from the beginning, but thicker in the course of time; it is not the case, as you suppose, that a person first filled a whole basin with serous residue, then next another with yellow bile, and then another with phlegm, and that only then is the black evacuated. From which it is clear that what is proper is attracted by the drug, while the watery matter floating on the surface follows along with it.

You can observe this now, even if you did not before: that people evacuate a very great quantity of watery and bilious matter [335] upon such doses of drugs, but that the total evacuation occurring in them upon the drugs that draw off black [bile] is very small. Yet according to your hypothesis, at any rate, the total quantity evacuated ought always to be greatest upon the drugs of black [bile], and least upon those of watery and bilious matter. For your account, I suppose, distinguished the kind of things evacuated by the weakness and strength of the drugs, as in the case of those that draw off black [bile]. And since these differ from the others in strength, the evacuation will be very copious: first of all the watery matter, then of the bilious, then of the phlegmatic, then of the black [bile] itself. With the weak downward purgatives, on the other hand, the watery matters alone will be evacuated. But none of these things is seen to happen, so that these observed phenomena overthrow your account. It is also right that you should answer why, if the thicker matters are always evacuated after the thinner, black bile is drawn before the blood, although it is a kind of sediment of the blood, as the lees are in wines.

[336] Perhaps, then, you will ask whether there is any drug that draws off blood straight from the outset. There is, my good friend, but no one would use it. Why? you will perhaps say. Because that would be to slaughter the person, not to purge him. For purging drugs are called purging by everyone for precisely this reason, that they render the blood clean of the residues I have mentioned. Surely no physician is so wise as to wish to evacuate all the blood while leaving the other humours in the body. Hence they count among the deleterious drugs all such as produce an evacuation of blood through the veins of the stomach and the intestines. Yet according to your hypothesis not even these ought to evacuate blood from the outset. As for the names of such drugs, even if I knew them with certainty I would not disclose them in my writings. But this much at least is safe for me to relate: what happened among the Bithynian Thracians while we were still boys. A certain man found an herb of such a kind that whoever took it excreted blood and so perished.

So, since many were dying in a similar [337] manner, they judged what was happening to deserve a more exacting investigation; they found the poisoner and brought him before the governor of the province. The governor made it his business not only to put the man himself to death but also to find out whether anyone else had either taught him or learned from him. The man said that he had learned of the plant from no one. Once, he said, while carrying a pig's liver to some suburban property, his belly became gripped, and he set the liver down on a herb. Then, picking it up again, he saw bloody ichors flowing out of the whole liver onto the herb. Conjecturing from this that the herb was likely to draw blood, he gave it, by way of trial, to some chance person, and when he found what he had expected, he used it thereafter for evil. He said, moreover, that he had not shown the herb to any other person either. This is what that poisoner said under very prolonged torture. In the account he gave of the herb he had said that it grew in great abundance everywhere round about. The governor of the province therefore ordered him to be led away blindfolded to his death, so that he might not point it out to anyone in the meantime.

So, my excellent friend, it is likely that many drugs have been discovered having such a [338] power as to draw blood right from the outset. But it is reasonable that they are passed over in silence, just as the other deleterious poisons are passed over in silence by all who have sense. For there have already been some who were unstinting even in the teaching of these things, displaying a kind of monstrous liberality in sharing and writing down the preparations of each of the deleterious poisons; but such men are not among those who have sense, just as you are not either, if you ask us which of the drugs are ones that draw off blood. Let us, then, bring the argument back again to the aim we had from the beginning. The man who says that all the humours are attracted equally, but that the most free-flowing are excreted first and the others after them, betrays what is dearest to him, since he admits that the attractive power exists among the things that are. Concerning this power his chorus behaves shamelessly, and has brought itself to say outlandish things about the separation of bile and of urine, about distribution and other such matters; and moreover he posits things contrary to the phenomena, as we showed earlier.

For if this hypothesis is true, the total evacuation will be greatest with the drugs that draw off black [bile], and least with those that draw off the serous [339] residues. And yet I will show you ten thousand times over, sophist, if you are willing, now at least, to behold the works of the art, that the greatest evacuation always follows the hydragogue drugs and the least follows those that purge out black [bile]. And I will show also that the black [bile] is evacuated right at the very beginning. So the one who says that all the humours are drawn equally is insensible and ignorant to this degree. As for the one who says that they are altered, let him see in his turn to what degree, on his view, it will make no difference whether one phlebotomises the jaundiced patient or purges him with a cholagogue drug. In the same way it is all one to phlebotomise the dropsical patient and to evacuate him with one of the hydragogues. Then are not such things shameful? The many, hearing such things as physicians contradict one another, wrongly laugh them to scorn; they have all condemned reasoning, and they call those who utter anything whatever about it 'word-doctors' (logiatroi). For what I am always accustomed to say, it is the right moment for me to say now too: every layman is better than a sophist of this sort.

For even if [340] nothing else, laymen at least preserve the natural notions, whereas the sophists destroy even these through bad habituations. Recently, at any rate, a layman who was not unintelligent, when ulcerous and discoloured eruptions had suddenly appeared on him over many parts of the body, came to the physician, asking to be purged as quickly as possible. And when the physician instead bade him be bled, 'Do not be mad,' he said, 'for it stands to reason that together with what is corrupted, what is good is evacuated as well.' But those who would rather anything be true than the Hippocratic account destroy the common notions too, through their love of contention. And then they leap upon us as if to tear us apart, yet are vexed by the refutations drawn from the works themselves. It would be just, however, that, as we bear with them when they abuse Hippocrates over things they do not know, and try to persuade them, so they too should endure the refutations, and preferably, if possible, feel affection for those who have taught them; or if not, at least not hate them altogether. At any rate, one of the physicians of this sort of senselessness, having heard that I had treated a great many by purging alone,

— namely, many of those who have the so-called [341] alōpekiai (alopeciae) — from then on began to hate me. Another likewise hated me because [I had treated] incipient cancerous conditions, the so-called elephantes and phagedainai, and many other malignant ulcers. Another, because I treated those subject to skotōma by purgations alone. Another, because I cured by purgations alone maniacal, epileptic and melancholic patients, and also not a few suffering from kephalaia, as well as sufferers from sciatica. In the same way I cured by purgations alone chronic pains scattered over many places. So too with the man recently treated for three months by the physicians as a colic patient, who was going from bad to worse: I ordered him to throw away all those [remedies] and cured him by purgations alone. I also cured by purgations alone the female flux of a woman not without distinction among the women in Rome. So too, in many other women of lesser note, I cured this very affection and certain others of those that arise in the womb. As for erysipelata, what need is there even to say that there is no more effective remedy than a bile-drawing drug, just as the drug that draws phlegm is most contrary to them?

I could go on for a whole day telling of other [342] marvellous results that followed upon purgations, of which those who have never learned the art concerning purgative drugs are, as one would expect, ignorant. For where they do not even believe that there is any purgative drug at all, how indeed will they understand in which cases one must use it, or in what manner? For this reason some others treat the affections guided by bare experience (peira) alone. But these clever fellows of ours, who also handle reason (logos), not in order to add something to what has been discovered through experience (empeiria) but to overturn even that, practise medicine far worse than those who set out from bare irrational routines alone. Of all these things the one beginning and source is the hatred of Hippocrates. From this source many other things have flowed, and also this very inquiry now before us, the one concerning the attractive power, of which the power of purgative drugs is a part, or a species, or whatever one may wish to call it.
